questions.prompt: Which kind of work is among the documented users of the libuv worker pool?

choices.text: All JavaScript array loops whenever they appear inside async functions.
Every object property lookup during a JSON response conversion.
Asynchronous filesystem operations such as a file read.
Every HTTP route callback body regardless of its contents.

questions.explanation: The worker pool serves selected native APIs. It is not an automatic executor for arbitrary JavaScript.

sources.title: Do Not Block the Event Loop or Worker Pool
sources.claim: Node offloads selected filesystem, dns.lookup, crypto and zlib operations to its worker pool; arbitrary JavaScript stays on its execution thread, and long worker tasks delay other queued jobs.

questions.prompt: Why can filesystem latency rise when expensive cryptographic jobs saturate the worker pool?

choices.text: Cryptographic jobs always block the OS network stack globally.
Promises must complete in their creation order before files can be read.
Selected crypto and filesystem operations compete for pooled workers.
Filesystem APIs are serialized through each HTTP client private thread.

questions.explanation: These API families use the finite pool. Long jobs can occupy workers needed by shorter jobs.

questions.prompt: A developer wraps a ten-second JavaScript calculation in Promise.resolve().then(calculate). What problem remains?

choices.text: The calculation still monopolizes its JS thread while it executes.
A Promise prevents any synchronous code in calculate from executing.
The Promise automatically runs calculate in an isolated worker thread.
The callback is automatically split into one-millisecond scheduled chunks.

questions.explanation: Scheduling a callback later does not change where its synchronous computation runs.

questions.prompt: Which improvement directly addresses a large synchronous calculation on the main loop?

choices.text: Rename the callback async without modifying the computation.
Wrap the result in a Promise only after the loop has finished.
Partition into yielding chunks or explicitly offload suitable computation.
Increase a request timeout so the loop is permitted to block longer.

questions.explanation: Partitioning or offloading changes resource use; timeout changes and naming do not.

questions.prompt: Which workload is a good candidate for Node worker_threads?

choices.text: Every JSON request regardless of actual processing cost.
A small property read that needs no noticeable CPU time.
CPU-intensive JavaScript with enough work to justify worker overhead.
An ordinary asynchronous socket read already handled efficiently by Node.

questions.explanation: Workers can run JavaScript in parallel and benefit CPU workloads. Built-in asynchronous I/O is usually more efficient than workers.

sources.title: Worker threads
sources.claim: Worker threads execute JavaScript in parallel and are useful for CPU-intensive work rather than ordinary asynchronous I/O.

questions.prompt: Why split an unusually large worker job into comparable-cost pieces?

choices.text: To ensure every piece bypasses the worker queue and executes immediately.
To make short queued jobs wait until all pieces of that large job finish.
To let pooled workers interleave shorter work instead of being occupied too long.
To avoid measuring task sizes because equal input lengths always cost equally.

questions.explanation: Long tasks reduce effective available capacity. Partitioning can improve fairness while still carrying overhead.

questions.prompt: Which operations use the documented libuv worker pool? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Selected asynchronous crypto operations.
Selected asynchronous filesystem operations.
All pure JavaScript loops solely because they return a Promise.
Every socket readiness event consumes a dedicated pooled worker.
Selected zlib operations.

questions.explanation: A: Correct: expensive native crypto can use workers. B: Correct: filesystem APIs are documented pool users. C: Incorrect: JavaScript syntax does not offload CPU work. D: Incorrect: the event loop uses nonblocking network mechanisms. E: Correct: compression APIs also use the pool.

questions.prompt: Which claims separate asynchronous scheduling from offloading? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A zero-delay timer preempts a currently running CPU loop.
Explicit worker execution can run CPU-heavy JavaScript away from the main loop.
Moving execution later does not itself move it to another thread.
An async function can contain blocking synchronous JavaScript.
A Promise callback automatically executes on a different processor.

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect: timers wait for callback execution to yield. B: Correct: worker_threads is an explicit parallel mechanism. C: Correct: thread choice remains unchanged. D: Correct: synchronous work still occupies the execution thread. E: Incorrect: callback scheduling is not a thread boundary.

questions.prompt: Which worker-thread design claims are supported? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Worker startup and communication have no performance costs at all.
A pool can avoid creating a new worker for every small task.
Workers can execute CPU-intensive JavaScript in parallel.
Workers necessarily outperform built-in asynchronous I/O for every file read.
A worker can communicate by passing messages.

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect: overhead must be considered. B: Correct: the documentation recommends pooling for repeated work. C: Correct: parallel JS is their purpose. D: Incorrect: Node asynchronous I/O is generally more efficient. E: Correct: message passing connects workers and their parent.

sources.title: Worker threads
sources.claim: Workers run parallel JavaScript, communicate by messages, have overhead and should be pooled for recurring tasks.

questions.prompt: Which decisions improve fairness with limited worker capacity? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Consider dividing highly variable jobs into bounded pieces.
Assume one occupied worker leaves exactly the same pool capacity available.
Recognize that expensive tasks can delay shorter queued jobs.
Accept arbitrarily long tasks because offloading removes all latency risks.
Account for partitioning overhead when choosing task size.

questions.explanation: A: Correct: bounded tasks allow interleaving. B: Incorrect: the occupied worker is unavailable for other tasks. C: Correct: long tasks reduce effective pool capacity. D: Incorrect: pooled capacity can still saturate. E: Correct: smaller pieces add scheduling and representation overhead.
